description:
Lunar Loop is a browser game in English, Russian and Azerbaijani. Players train as astronauts on the real rim of Shackleton crater at the Moon’s south pole. The terrain, sunlight, shadows and Earth visibility all come from NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) data.

Every choice has a cost. Steep slopes burn oxygen. Shadowed areas drain power for heating. Solar panels only work where the real horizon lets the Sun through. You can only reach Earth where the Earth clears the hills.
summary: Lunar Loop is a free browser game in which kids aged 7–13 run a small base on the real rim of Shackleton crater, at the Moon's south pole, for 28 days. Each morning they share out limited solar power between life support, a greenhouse, a science lab, a radio to Earth and a storm shelter, and on some days they decide whether to trade oxygen for a moonwalk. No choice is free, and every gauge previews tomorrow before they commit. The game runs on real NASA data: sunlight and Earth visibility are computed from LRO laser-altimeter terrain; solar storms come from NASA DONKI (saved periods from 2012–2024, or the last 28 days, live); which days are storm days, and how strong, comes from LRO CRaTER radiation measurements in NASA's OSDR RadLab; and lessons cite OSDR studies. Players wait out the real 1.3-second radio delay to Earth. A guided tutorial, touch support, three languages (English, Russian, Azerbaijani) and class mission codes make it easy to use at home or in school. It turns the trade-offs mission planners face into decisions a child can make, and explains the real science behind each one.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Loop is a browser game about running a Moon base, made for kids aged 7–13. The player commands a small outpost on the real rim of Shackleton crater at the lunar south pole for 28 days. Every morning brings a limited amount of power: what is left in the battery plus today's sunlight. The player shares it out between six systems, each with a real cost:

• Air & heat (life support): 2 power, or 3 on dark, cold days. Too little, and the air gets worse tomorrow.

• Greenhouse (food production): 1 power = 1 food; the crew eats 1 food a day.

• Science lab: makes science points, which only count once the radio sends them home.

• Radio to Earth (communication): works only when Earth is above the real hills. It sends science and brings storm warnings. Players wait the real 1.3-second light delay each way (Mars would be 3–22 minutes).

• Storm shelter (radiation shielding): cuts the dose to a fifth, but costs 2 power and halves greenhouse and lab work.

• Moonwalk (on some days): +3 science, but it uses suit oxygen and adds radiation (double in a storm). This is the challenge's "oxygen for research" trade.

Morning dilemmas (Moon dust on the panels, an air leak, a micrometeoroid hit, a broken pump) ask "fix it now or live with it?", and cargo landers on Days 8, 15 and 22 offer one of three upgrade crates (bigger battery, water-wall shielding, grow lights, relay satellite…). A live drawing of the base reacts to every choice, and every gauge shows tomorrow's value before the player commits. Ending early is never a "game over": Mission Control brings the crew home and explains why, with a tip and a 28-day chart.

HOW NASA DATA DRIVES IT

• Sunlight and Earth contact: computed every two hours from NASA LRO LOLA terrain (5 m and 40 m elevation models) with our own horizon model. It matches NASA's published average-illumination map (r = 0.963). This gives the real polar problem: hills hide the low Sun for days, and the Earth too.

• Solar storms: NASA DONKI flares and solar energetic particle events from 12 real 28-day periods (2012–2024), or the last 28 days downloaded live in the browser, each labelled "saved" or "live".

• Radiation: NASA OSDR RadLab. Daily LRO CRaTER measurements in lunar orbit decide which days are storm days and how strong (for example 3,550 times normal on 24 January 2012), so storms last as long as the real radiation stayed high. Artemis I (inside Orion) and Curiosity (on Mars) measurements appear as facts. CRaTER agrees with the Chang'e-4 surface value for the same weeks (12.9 vs 13.2 μGy per hour).

• Biology: NASA OSDR studies OSD-268 (lettuce grown on the ISS) and OSD-146 (radiation and the gut microbiome) in the food and radiation lessons. NASA-STD-3001 gives the 600 mSv career limit for scale.

Every number in the game is labelled measured, computed or simulated, and an in-game Research Database explains every dataset, how it was processed and what it changes in play.

FOR KIDS, FAMILIES AND CLASSROOMS

A guided tutorial day with a Mission Control coach teaches each system by having the child do it. Plain language, with terms such as radiation dose, mSv and EVA explained when they first appear. Big touch buttons that work on phones and tablets. English, Russian and Azerbaijani. Two levels: Cadet (7–9, with a suggested plan) and Commander (10+, only life support filled in). Mission codes let a whole class play exactly the same dates and compare strategies. Older players can try the 3D astronaut trainer on the same real terrain.

TESTING AND BALANCE

We play-tested with 120 simulated missions per strategy. On Commander level, careful planning completes 95 and spending everything completes 11. Never sheltering loses 38 crews to radiation. On Cadet, the suggested plan plus sheltering on warnings completes 118. The game was played through in all three languages, on desktop and phone layouts.

TOOLS

JavaScript (ES modules), three.js r170 (3D), esbuild (bundling), Node.js scripts to download and process the NASA data, SVG and Canvas for the base drawing and charts, and the Web Audio API for procedural sound. It runs in any modern browser with no install or account, as one offline HTML file or as a static website.

AI USE

Built with the help of an AI assistant, Claude (Anthropic): code, text, translations, data processing, and the procedural graphics and sounds. This is stated in the game's main menu, its credits, the Moon Base data card, the README and the page metadata. The NASA data is used unchanged, and no NASA logos or branding are used.
